name: Stamulumab

lead: Stamulumab (MYO-029) is a monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, the protein that restrains muscle growth. Muscle-minded readers mention it as an early attempt at removing the body's growth brake for a fuller physique.

It binds myostatin in the blood so the protein cannot activate its receptor on muscle cells, which should allow more muscle growth. Wyeth tested it in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies.

paras: It is not available. Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would stop developing it for muscular dystrophy, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.
Published sources reviewed do not detail its safety results. It is an unapproved, discontinued investigational antibody.

angle.text: Stamulumab is a discontinued antibody that binds myostatin to lift the body's brake on muscle growth, aimed at more muscle and a fuller physique. It was tested in muscular dystrophy rather than for physique, and development stopped in 2008.

lead: Stamulumab (MYO-029) is an experimental monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, a protein that limits muscle growth. It was developed by Wyeth as a possible treatment for muscular dystrophy [1].

It was tested in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies [2][3]. Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would not continue developing it for muscular dystrophy [1]. It was never approved, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.

paras: Stamulumab binds myostatin so that it cannot signal through its receptor, removing a brake on muscle growth [1].

Wyeth tested the drug in Collegeville, Pennsylvania. A phase 1/2 multiple-ascending-dose trial ran from 2005 to 2006 in people with facioscapulohumeral, Becker and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, and the results were published in Annals of Neurology in May 2008 [1]. Wyeth stated in March 2008 that it would pursue myostatin inhibition by other approaches [1].

A phase 1 study (72 healthy participants, begun 2004) evaluated safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics [2]. A phase 1/2 study (108 adults with Becker, facioscapulohumeral or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, begun 2005) was completed [3]. Wikipedia notes the trial contained some measures of efficacy but does not report the findings [1].

timeline.event: Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers begins [2].
Phase 1/2 trial in adult muscular dystrophy begins [3].
Wyeth announces it will not develop the drug further for muscular dystrophy; results published [1].
